title: Tier I Checkpoint II — Building a Unit

pts: Pick one overarching can-do outcome the whole unit builds toward, before choosing a single activity.
Every lesson planned inside this unit gets checked against this aim, not just against its own local content.
The unit's cumulative task is written directly from this aim, before anything else is drafted.

items: Read the whole textbook unit (Unit 11).
Ask what learners could do by the end that they could not do at the start.
Draft a can-do aim and a cumulative task.
Check the aim against learners’ needs: water shortage is a real local issue many learners know about.
Share the aim with learners on day one.
For a younger class: Learners can say how they use water at home and one way to save it.
Not applicable (planning step).

blocks.x: The unit aim and final task:

lines: Aim: Learners can describe a local water problem and give advice to solve it, in speech and writing.
Final task: groups present a short ‘water-saving campaign’ to another class, with a poster and a two-minute talk.
L1 vocabulary of water use; L2 reading on rivers; L3 present continuous to describe what is happening now; L4 should/shouldn’t for advice; L5 planning the campaign; L6 presenting.

body: Purpose: the finished one-page plan (built up through this unit). Content: an A4 landscape table with six columns (L1–L6) and rows for ‘aim’, ‘skills’, ‘language’, ‘support/stretch’, ‘homework’. A banner across the top with the unit aim, and a flag at the right end labelled ‘final task: campaign’. Style: clean, colour-coded rows. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free). A shared unit-plan template.

blocks.x: The one-page plan on A4, kept in the front of the textbook.

pts: Decide whether this unit leans structural, functional, lexical or task-based, given the outcome just set.
The choice shapes what gets foregrounded — a grammar point, a function, a set of collocations, or a real-world task.
Naming the lens explicitly prevents the unit from drifting between logics without anyone deciding to.

items: Identify the textbook’s lens: structural (present continuous, should) with a reading-skills strand.
Decide whether to add another lens. Here, a task-based lens fits: the campaign is a real-world task.
Keep the structural points but let them serve the task.
Record the blend on the plan.
A functional lens (giving advice, describing problems) would also fit this unit.
Not applicable (planning step).

lines: Structural backbone: present continuous; should/shouldn’t.
Task-based frame: every lesson moves towards the campaign.
Skills strand: reading (river text), speaking and writing (campaign).

body: Purpose: to show the syllabus mix for this unit. Content: a small wheel divided into three coloured segments: ‘structure’, ‘task’, ‘skills’, with the task segment slightly larger. Style: consistent with Figure 12.6. Board version: not applicable.

items: None needed.

points.h: Build From the Coursebook, Not Around It
pts: Audit the relevant coursebook unit against the aim: what to keep, what to add, what to cut.
Personalise at least one core activity to the specific class, rather than using every example as printed.
Decide upfront whether any lesson in this unit goes fully off-book.

items: Omit: one of two gap-fill exercises on the present continuous.
Add: a pair survey on water use at home (speaking).
Adapt: the reading comprehension questions become a pair quiz, and one question asks about a local river.
Personalize: examples use learners’ own town and river.
Note the changes in the teacher’s copy.
If the textbook has a listening activity with no audio, the teacher reads the script.
Support: the pair quiz includes picture clues.
Stretch: an extra question comparing two rivers.

lines: Textbook: People are throwing plastic into the river.
Personalized: In our town, people are washing clothes near the tank. The water is getting dirty.
How many buckets of water does your family use in a day? Where does your water come from? Is there ever a shortage?

body: Purpose: to show adaptation decisions. Content: three small textbook pages side by side, marked with a crossed-out exercise (‘omit’), a sticky note labelled ‘pair survey’ (‘add’), and a rewritten question (‘adapt’). Style: consistent with Figure 13.2. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free). An adaptations log per unit.

blocks.x: Sticky notes in the teacher’s copy.

points.h: Place It on the Scheme of Work
pts: Slot the unit into the term map, backward-planned from its cumulative task and the term's larger outcome.
Build in at least one review touchpoint inside the unit, not just at the end of the term.
Mark where this unit's formative checkpoint (Unit 11) will fall on the calendar.

items: Locate the unit on the term plan: weeks 6–7.
Check events: a school holiday falls on day 3 of week 7.
Plan six lessons across seven teaching days, keeping one lesson flexible.
Place a mid-unit checkpoint after lesson 3 (Unit 11).
Note that the review week (week 8) will recycle this unit’s language.
If the term is behind, compress lessons 1 and 2 into one and keep the campaign.
Not applicable (planning step).

lines: Week 6: Mon L1, Tue L2, Thu L3 + checkpoint, Fri L4.
Week 7: Mon L5, Tue flexible, Thu L6 (presentations). Wed holiday.

body: Purpose: to locate the unit in the term. Content: a strip of the term plan with weeks 6–7 highlighted, the six lessons marked, a holiday shaded grey and a small checkpoint flag after L3. Style: consistent with Figure 14.1. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free) term plan.

points.h: Plan for the Range in the Room
pts: Design the unit's core task with built-in scaffolding and stretch from day one, not as a later add-on.
Plan at least one open-ended activity across the unit so every learner can perform at their own level.
Decide grouping patterns for each lesson in advance, varied deliberately across the unit.

items: For the reading lesson, prepare three task levels (Unit 15).
For writing the campaign poster, prepare three scaffold levels: full frame, starters, word bank.
Plan open-ended tasks: List as many ways to save water as you can.
Assign flexible groups: mixed ability for the campaign; similar ability for one grammar support session.
Give each group member a role (writer, designer, speaker, checker), rotating.
Offer confident speakers a stretch role: answering questions from the audience.
The whole step is differentiation.

blocks.x: Three scaffold levels for the poster text:

lines: Frame: In our town, people are ______. This is a problem because ______. You should ______.
Starters: Every day… / This is bad because… / Please…
Word bank: waste, tap, leak, save, bucket, shortage, should, shouldn’t

body: Purpose: to show group roles. Content: four learners around a poster, each with a small badge: ‘writer’, ‘designer’, ‘speaker’, ‘checker’. Style: inclusive, friendly. Board version: not applicable.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for groups with device access.

pts: Adjust activity length, the role of play, and metacognitive demand to whether this is a young-learner or adult class.
Match motivational framing (Unit 2 and Unit 16) to the actual age group and their real reasons for learning.
Recheck literacy assumptions if the unit involves any written self-study component.

items: Consider teenagers’ sensitivity to public correction (Unit 16): use delayed, anonymous feedback.
Build on teenage interests: invite learners to include a short slogan or rhyme in their campaign.
Allow choice of role within groups.
Frame motivation around real impact: the campaign will be shown to a younger class.
For adults, the same unit might become a letter to the local municipal office.
Support: shy learners can choose the designer or checker role.
Stretch: confident learners lead the presentation.

blocks.x: A campaign slogan in English and a home language, side by side, can be a proud part of the poster:

lines: Save every drop — it’s our future. (with a Kannada or Urdu version beneath, written by learners)

body: Purpose: a sample final product. Content: a hand-made poster with a tap and water drops, an English slogan at the top, a short home-language line beneath, three bullet points of advice using should, and a small group-member list at the bottom. Style: realistic student work, colourful. Board version: not applicable. Note: the home-language line should be written by a native speaker for the final artwork.

items: None needed.

body: Allowing learners to include their home language alongside English in a product like a poster is fully consistent with NEP 2020’s emphasis on multilingualism, and it often raises the quality of the English, because learners are proud of the whole piece and take more care over it.

points.h: Design for the Room You Have
pts: If the class is large, build in peer monitoring and choral techniques from the unit's very first lesson.
Plan instructions to be visual as well as spoken throughout the unit, not just in the first lesson.
Decide the marking-load strategy for this unit's written work before it's assigned, not after it's collected.

items: Form ten groups of four and one of two using bench groupings (turning to the bench behind).
Appoint group checkers with a checklist for each lesson.
Put instructions on the board with icons for each stage.
For presentations, split the class: half the groups present in lesson 6 to the other half, then swap, so all groups present within one period.
Use a marking rota: detailed feedback on posters from five groups per day.
If space allows, groups present standing at the front in pairs of groups.
Not applicable (classroom organization).

blocks.x: A presentation rotation for a large class:

lines: Round 1 (15 min): groups 1–5 present to groups 6–10 in five simultaneous clusters.
Round 2 (15 min): groups 6–10 present to groups 1–5.
Teacher circulates with a short rubric, visiting each cluster.

body: Purpose: to show presenting in a large class. Content: a classroom plan with five clusters; in each, one group stands presenting a poster to another group seated. The teacher moves between clusters with a clipboard. Style: clean plan view. Board version: not applicable.

items: A phone timer visible to all or projected.

blocks.x: A clap or bell to switch rounds.

pts: Plan one digital resource and one homework task that genuinely extend the unit, not just repeat its content.
Space the homework across the unit's timeline rather than assigning it all at once.
Build in a lightweight feedback loop for whatever is assigned, so the extension work retains its value.

items: Plan short, spaced homework linked to each lesson (Unit 19).
Include one real-world task: a water-use survey at home.
Include extensive reading on two days.
Offer a digital option (a short video on water saving) with an offline equivalent (a printed article).
Check homework briefly at the start of each lesson.
Include a home-language interview: ask a grandparent how water was collected when they were young; report in English.
Support: shorter tasks with frames.
Stretch: an optional mini-report comparing two households.

lines: After L1: count and record how many buckets your family uses in one day.
After L2: read two pages of your class reader.
After L3: write three sentences about what is happening in a photo of your street (present continuous).
After L4: write three pieces of advice for your family (should).
After L5: find one fact about water in your state (textbook, newspaper or online).

body: Plan your next textbook unit using the eight steps of this checkpoint. Put the result on one page and share it with a colleague who teaches the same grade. Ask them to point out one step they would do differently.

dek: Unit 20 of 100: closing this stretch of Tier I by drafting one full unit end-to-end, showing exactly where Units 11 through 19 meet in a single piece of real planning.

aims.x: This checkpoint unit brings Units 11–19 together by planning one complete unit of work from start to finish. The worked example is a six-lesson unit called ‘Water in our lives’ for a Grade 8 class at around A2–B1, but the steps apply to any unit, level or textbook.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: plan a unit from its aim to its homework, using every step in Units 11–19;
justify each planning decision with reference to learners and context;
adapt the worked example to your own class;
produce a one-page unit plan that colleagues can use.

why: Why this matters. Unit 10 proved the single-lesson foundations combine. This checkpoint proves the same for the unit-and-course-level foundations built since — before Tier I's final stretch.

background.x: Unit 10 showed that the foundations of a single lesson work together. This checkpoint does the same for the unit and the course. The questions are larger: what should a sequence of six lessons achieve, how does it fit into a term, how does it serve forty learners with different abilities and needs, and what happens between lessons?

The worked example is deliberately realistic. The class is a Grade 8 English class of forty-two learners in a Karnataka government school. Most learners speak Kannada at home; some speak Urdu or Telugu. The diagnostic grid (Unit 2) shows most learners around A2 for listening and reading, a small group at A1 in writing, and a few confident B1 speakers. The textbook unit is on the environment, with a reading passage about rivers and a grammar focus on the present continuous and should for advice. The term plan gives the unit two weeks.
Each of the eight points below takes one step of the planning process and shows how the decision was made. The result, summarized in the final art brief, is a one-page unit plan.

items: Campaign rubric. Assess the final task with three criteria: describes the problem clearly (present continuous), gives appropriate advice (should), and presents confidently as a group.
Checkpoint results. Record the mid-unit check and the changes made to lessons 4–6 as a result.
Homework completion. Track completion of the five unit tasks.
Self-assessment. Learners rate themselves against the unit aim at the start and end of the unit.
Which of the eight planning steps do you already do? Which do you usually skip?
How long would it take you to produce a one-page plan like this for your next unit? Is it worth it?
Which step made the biggest difference to the worked example? Would it be the same in your class?
How would you change the unit for a class of eighty? For a class of twelve?
What would convince you that the unit achieved its aim?

terms.def: A learner-created output, such as a campaign poster, that uses both English and a home language side by side, valuing learners’ languages as a resource.
A final task at the end of a unit that draws on all the language and skills taught, such as a group presentation or campaign.
Specific responsibilities assigned to members of a group, such as leader, note-taker, timekeeper or reporter, to structure participation and reduce free riding.
A planned short check partway through a unit of work, used to see whether learners are on track and to adjust the remaining lessons.

A presentation format in which several groups present at the same time to different small audiences, then rotate. It gives every group more speaking time and more listeners than whole-class presentations in a large class.

The deliberate combination of two or more syllabus types, such as topic, task, skills and structural strands, within a unit plan, recorded so that the unit’s main organizing principle and supporting strands are clear.
A written plan for a unit of work, setting out its aims, syllabus blend, lesson sequence, assessment checkpoints and final task or product.
